title: Waves

hints: Recall the definition of a transverse wave in terms of the direction of particle vibration P relative to the direction of energy propagation Q.
walkthrough: B1: For transverse wave, vibration perpendicular to propagation, so P perpendicular to Q.
teacher_walkthrough: The defining property of a transverse wave is that the particle vibration is at right angles to the direction of energy transfer. Here $P$ is the vibration direction and $Q$ is the propagation direction, so for a transverse wave $P$ is perpendicular to $Q$.
common_pitfalls: Confusing transverse with longitudinal and stating parallel.
Describing P and Q as opposite rather than stating the angle between them.

hints: Recall the definition of a longitudinal wave in terms of the direction of particle vibration P relative to the direction of energy propagation Q.
walkthrough: B1: For longitudinal wave, vibration parallel to propagation, so P parallel to Q (along same line).
teacher_walkthrough: The defining property of a longitudinal wave is that the particle vibration is along the same line as the direction of energy transfer. Here $P$ is the vibration direction and $Q$ is the propagation direction, so for a longitudinal wave $P$ is parallel to $Q$.
common_pitfalls: Stating perpendicular by reversing the two wave types.
Saying the lines are the same point rather than parallel lines.

hints: Identify the wave equation linking speed $v$, frequency $f$ and wavelength $\lambda$ for sound.
Convert the frequency from kHz to Hz before substituting $v$ and $f$ into the rearranged equation $\lambda = v/f$.
teacher_walkthrough: The wave speed is governed by $$v = f \lambda$$ Rearranged for wavelength: $$\lambda = \frac{v}{f}$$ Convert frequency: $$f = 1.7 \text{ kHz} = 1.7 \times 10^3 \text{ Hz} = 1700 \text{ Hz}$$ Substitute: $$\lambda = \frac{340}{1700}$$ Evaluate: $$\lambda = 0.20 \text{ m}$$
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to convert 1.7 kHz to 1700 Hz, giving a factor of 1000 error.
Inverting the formula to lambda = f / v.

hints: Recall that a closed end must be a displacement node and the open end is an antinode A, then count how many quarter wavelengths fit between the open antinode and the closed node using Fig. 5.1 with two antinodes.
teacher_walkthrough: For a tube closed at one end, the closed end is a node and the open end is an antinode. The separation between an adjacent antinode and node is $$\frac{\lambda}{4}$$ From Fig. 5.1, going from the open end to the closed end the pattern is antinode to node to antinode to node. That is three quarter wavelength sections: $$L = 3 \times \frac{\lambda}{4} = \frac{3\lambda}{4}$$ Substitute $\lambda = 0.20 \text{ m}$: $$L = 0.75 \times 0.20$$ $$L = 0.15 \text{ m}$$
common_pitfalls: Assuming L equals one full wavelength or one half wavelength instead of counting nodes and antinodes.
Confusing open and closed end conditions and using L = lambda/2.

hints: Recall the fundamental (lowest frequency, longest wavelength) mode of a closed tube has only one antinode at the open end and one node at the closed end, so L equals one quarter wavelength.
walkthrough: A1: lambda_max = 4 x L = 4 x 0.15 = 0.60 m.
teacher_walkthrough: The longest possible stationary wavelength corresponds to the fundamental mode. For a tube closed at one end: $$L = \frac{\lambda_{max}}{4}$$ Rearranged: $$\lambda_{max} = 4L$$ Substitute $L = 0.15 \text{ m}$: $$\lambda_{max} = 4 \times 0.15$$ $$\lambda_{max} = 0.60 \text{ m}$$
common_pitfalls: Using the open tube fundamental L = lambda/2 instead of L = lambda/4.
Thinking the given mode with two antinodes is already the longest wavelength.

hints: Apply Malus law for polarised light: transmitted intensity equals incident intensity times cos squared of the angle between the incident polarisation direction and the transmission axis.
teacher_walkthrough: Malus law for already polarised light incident on a polariser is $$I = I_0 \cos^2 \theta$$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the incident polarisation and the transmission axis. Here $I_0 = 8.5 \text{ W m}^{-2}$ and $\theta = 35^{\circ}$: $$I = 8.5 \times \cos^2(35^{\circ})$$ Evaluate $\cos(35^{\circ})$: $$\cos(35^{\circ}) = 0.8192$$ Square it: $$\cos^2(35^{\circ}) = 0.8192^2 = 0.6710$$ Multiply: $$I = 8.5 \times 0.6710 = 5.70 \text{ W m}^{-2}$$ This shows the transmitted intensity is $5.7 \text{ W m}^{-2}$.
common_pitfalls: Using cos instead of cos squared, or using Malus law for unpolarised light I0/2.
Calculator in radian mode when evaluating cos 35 degrees.

hints: Identify that the light incident on the second filter has intensity $5.7 \text{ W m}^{-2}$ and is polarised along the first filter axis, so the relevant angle in Malus law is the angle between the two transmission axes.
Set up $5.2 = 5.7 \cos^2(\alpha - 35^{\circ})$ and rearrange to find $\cos(\alpha - 35^{\circ})$ by dividing then square rooting.
walkthrough: C1: 5.2 = 5.7 cos^2 theta, giving theta = alpha - 35 deg = 17 deg.
teacher_walkthrough: Apply Malus law at the second filter. Incident intensity $I_0 = 5.7 \text{ W m}^{-2}$, transmitted $I = 5.2 \text{ W m}^{-2}$: $$I = I_0 \cos^2 \phi$$ where $\phi$ is the angle between the two transmission axes, $\phi = \alpha - 35^{\circ}$. So: $$5.2 = 5.7 \times \cos^2 \phi$$ Divide: $$\cos^2 \phi = \frac{5.2}{5.7} = 0.9123$$ Square root: $$\cos \phi = \sqrt{0.9123} = 0.9551$$ Inverse cosine: $$\phi = \cos^{-1}(0.9551) = 17.2^{\circ}$$ Hence: $$\alpha = 35^{\circ} + \phi = 35^{\circ} + 17.2^{\circ} = 52^{\circ}$$
common_pitfalls: Using 35 degrees directly as the angle for the second filter instead of the difference alpha minus 35 degrees.
Forgetting to square root after dividing, or forgetting to add the 35 degrees back to get alpha.
